entries.title: Nametags, and a messenger
notes: !antiragdoll keeps you on your feet. Games ragdoll you four different ways and stopping one of them is not stopping any of them, so this holds the humanoid's states, its platform-stand and the joints themselves -- and stands down while you are flying or seated rather than fighting whatever put you there.

Nametags. Anybody else running the hub in your server gets a small tag above them: their face, their name, how long they have been a hub user, and the hub's mark -- drawn in THEIR theme, so somebody on red reads as red. One fixed size with a distance cap, so a crowded server does not turn into a wall of cards. Hover one for view, teleport, profile and chat.

A Roblox client cannot read another client's script state, so the tags go through a relay -- and it was built not to be able to read what it holds. What it stores is a digest of the place and server id pointing at encrypted bytes; it never learns which game anybody is in, who they are, or what any message says.

Private messages between hub users. Sealed on your machine and opened on theirs, so the relay and anyone who takes that server sees bytes. Stated plainly on the screen where you type: it does NOT protect you from another script on your own machine, because the key has to live in the executor's config.

Messaging asks first. A first approach is a request the other person accepts or blocks, because a mailbox address can be worked out from a user id -- consent is the thing stopping anyone writing to anyone. Blocks last across restarts, and both people asking at once is treated as agreement rather than two prompts.

!chats is a proper chat system: a draggable window that collapses to a puck and remembers where you left it, a list of every conversation with unread counts, message bubbles with real Roblox headshots, and an emoji picker -- Roblox has no emoji keyboard and the operating system's does not reach a game text box.

Group chats. Each group gets its own key, made once and handed to every member inside an envelope sealed to them alone; messages go out sealed with it to each member's mailbox. The relay learns nothing new -- a shared group mailbox would have meant telling it who is in the room. Add people, rename it, and see who said what.

Messages reach anyone, anywhere. Message a hub user by their Roblox username whether or not they are in your server or even online -- anything sent while they are away waits in their mailbox and arrives when they next execute. If they have never run the hub it says so rather than sending into the void.

Online status. A green or grey dot on every conversation, and the header saying online or last seen 5m ago, with 'messages will wait' when they are away. The relay only remembers when a mailbox last checked in.
A request waits up to 7 days, shows greyed out with its countdown, and then expires -- a question nobody answered in a week is not still being considered.
Chat settings, in the chat window: message notifications on or off, message requests on or off, and the blocked list with unblock a tap away.

Catch up. The first mail sweep after you execute tells you what arrived while you were gone in one line rather than a toast per message, and the overview shows a catch-up card when messages are waiting.
Show my own tag, in nametag settings. Your tag above your own head, built from what the hub actually publishes about you, so it is what everybody else sees rather than a mock-up of it.

The Spotify card no longer opens itself. It used to reappear whenever music started AND on every track change -- closing it only bought you until the next song. It stays shut until you open it and remembers that; !spotify auto turns the old behaviour back on.
Infinite Yield's chat command is now say, which was already its alias -- with a messenger in the hub, chat read as the wrong thing. chat still works, so nothing that used it breaks.

Theme changes reach other people's screens straight away instead of after ten or fifteen seconds. A change is pushed the moment it happens, coalesced so flicking through the picker is one update rather than ten.

entries.title: An AI companion, MCP, the overview screen and sound
notes: The hub opens on an overview rather than a bare bar. Where you are with the game's own art, how full the server is, the weather and the time, your friends with their faces and what they are playing -- with a Join on the ones you can reach -- who is in this server with you, and what you were doing last time, all on one screen. The resume prompt and the guide moved into it instead of stacking up as separate things to dismiss.

!translate reads the chat in whatever language it arrives in and puts English under it, keeping the original above so you can check it. It can follow one person, translate into any of eighteen languages, and !trsay sends what you type in theirs.

An AI companion, on !ai. It opens a panel laid out like a chat app -- conversations down the left, the exchange in the middle, a detail pane on the right that stays shut until a card sends something to it -- and it can actually reach the game. Twelve tools: look at the server, read a player, search the chat log, read a player's session history, read the developer console, list and run hub commands, run Luau, search ScriptBlox, control Spotify, and report what the hub itself currently has switched on. Bring a key from OpenAI, Claude, DeepSeek or OpenRouter; the model list is fetched live from whichever you use, with its real context sizes and, on OpenRouter, its real prices.

Manual gates the two tools that DO something and leaves reads alone, because making 'who is in this server' cost two taps is friction rather than approval. Auto trusts the model's own confirm flag on code -- and a missing flag gates rather than runs. Two things the model never decides either way: a command this game punishes always waits for you, from the list the hub already keeps, and running a ScriptBlox script always takes your tap.

It answers rather than opening things. A command whose only effect is putting a panel on screen -- !chatlog, !profile, !overview, !cmds -- is refused with the name of the tool that actually answers, so the model corrects itself inside the same turn instead of handing you a window to read.

!esp and !aim take their options as arguments now: !esp skeleton, !esp boxes on, !esp chams off, !aim silent, !aim on. They used to open their panel and throw the word away, which looked exactly like having worked.

The panel renders markdown, because models write it whether or not you ask. Bold, italic, code, headings, bullets and links become Roblox rich text -- escaped first, since one stray angle bracket in prose would otherwise blank the whole message.

Token counts, what the conversation has cost, and what is left on the key sit in the header. The balance is real where the provider publishes one -- OpenRouter and DeepSeek do -- and simply absent where they do not, rather than guessed. The model names each chat itself once the first reply lands.

Announcing an action and then not taking it is caught. If a reply ends on an undertaking with no tool call behind it, the loop asks once for the follow-through. There is no cap on tool rounds any more; the send button becomes a stop button instead, and a request already in flight is dropped rather than allowed to land in the middle of the next question.

!mcp hands the same twelve tools to a model outside the game -- Claude Code, Cursor, anything that speaks MCP. Roblox cannot host a server, so a small bridge runs on your machine and the hub polls it; the setup panel carries the fetch line, the register line, and a prompt you can paste to let your own model do the whole thing. It checks whether the bridge is there before connecting, remembers once you have one so it never shows install steps twice, and tells the bridge to close when you turn it off or unload the hub. Outside calls are gated exactly as the panel's are.

Executing the hub again replaces it. Its windows are parented outside PlayerGui and survive a re-execute, so every run used to add another complete hub -- and the oldest one answered your keypresses, which from inside the game is indistinguishable from the new code not having loaded.

MCP has no on and off. Being in the game is what those meant, so the hub simply looks for a bridge and connects to one the moment it answers -- backing off while there is nothing there, and hurrying the moment you open the panel so you watch it connect rather than waiting out a gap. Losing the bridge puts it back to looking.

The bridge quit the instant its stdin closed, which is what happens when you background it or redirect it: it printed the line saying it was listening and then was not. It keeps the queue up now whether or not a client is attached to it.

A bridge that is running but out of reach now says so. Every failed call comes back as words -- what threw, or which HTTP code came back -- and the panel prints it instead of waiting with a blank face. Two ways in as well: request() is the one that can POST, and where an executor refuses loopback through it, HttpGet is tried for the health check that decides whether a bridge is there at all. The same machine's two names are both tried, since executors disagree about which of localhost and 127.0.0.1 they will resolve.

Six more tools: how the game is running, what the script hub has going, who on your friends list is online and which of them are here, a message onto your screen, a message into the game's chat, and translation. Eighteen in total, and speaking in chat waits for you in either mode -- everyone in the server reads it under your name.
The MCP panel is one thing to copy, and it is a prompt rather than a command. Setting the bridge up is four steps of shell work the model on the other end can do itself, so it does.

MCP stopped being flaky. A single failed poll was treated as the bridge disappearing, so one slow frame said it had gone and a second later it was back; it now takes a run of them. The client is named when it connects -- 'connected to Claude Code' rather than 'connected' -- announced once for the session rather than every time a client re-initialises, which some do per request. And anything a model does through the bridge that CHANGES something puts a toast on screen carrying the AI mark; reads stay quiet, because a model looking at the server four times to answer one question would bury the screen.

Two MCP clients can run at once. The bridge bound its port unconditionally, so the first client to start owned it and every one after that died with EADDRINUSE -- which the client reports as 'Connection closed'. The HTTP side is the rendezvous with the game and only one copy needs it; the rest forward their clients' calls to whichever copy has it, and if that one leaves, the next takes the port over rather than staying broken.

The bridge keeps itself current. On the owner's launch it fetches the published copy and writes it in place if it moved -- taking effect the next time your client starts it, rather than swapping the file under a live conversation. If the hub sees a version it was not written against it says so once, in a modal carrying the prompt that updates it and a way to carry on regardless. Out of date is not broken.

The bridge's call endpoint is no longer reachable from a web page. Loopback is not a boundary -- any site the user visits can fetch a 127.0.0.1 URL -- so the endpoint that runs a tool now needs a secret kept in a file only they can read, and every endpoint refuses a request carrying the headers a browser attaches. Found by a review of the commit that introduced it, before anyone shipped against it.

The out-of-date bridge warning is built like the resume prompt now: a row per choice with its mark, a line saying what it does and its own button, and the same checkbox for not being asked again -- rather than a paragraph with the buttons somewhere else.

MCP tool calls no longer stop the heartbeat. Jobs ran inline in the poll loop, so five at once -- or one approval prompt sat waiting on a person -- meant the bridge stopped hearing from the game and told the model it had disconnected, which was a lie that sent people off to fix something that was not broken. Each job runs on its own thread now and answers from there; the poll does nothing but poll.

run_code reports its own output. LogService delivers a print a frame after it happens, and the output was collected the instant the code returned -- so anything that finished promptly said 'ran clean' with its prints nowhere, and the only way to see them was to ask for the console separately.

The bridge tells the client when the toolbox fills. It advertised listChanged and never sent one, so a session that listed tools before the game connected kept the placeholder for good -- no amount of turning MCP on changed what it could see.

The bridge updates itself atomically and refuses a publish that does not compile. It wrote over itself in place, so an interruption mid-write left half a file and a client that only ever said 'Connection closed'.

Every bridge endpoint now checks the Host header, which is the standard guard against a page reaching loopback under a name the browser trusts. A late answer to a call that already timed out is dropped rather than kept forever, and a job queued before the game dropped is discarded rather than run minutes later in a different server.
An approval prompt that nobody answered says so, rather than reporting that the user declined.

The card for code the model is running says Running code, and the friend tag in the overview is a small outlined label in the corner like the player count, rather than a filled pill sat on the artwork.

Everything new works on a phone. MouseEnter never fires on touch, so the quick actions on a name and the delete on a conversation -- both hover-only -- did not exist there; they are simply present on touch now, at a size a finger can hit, with the chips after them starting past them rather than underneath. And floating panels are scaled to the screen the way the modals always were, which nothing had needed while the widest was 470 and the AI panel is 720 -- wider than a phone held upright. Its conversation rail starts closed there, since it would otherwise be most of the width.

Spotify follows the music again. The card built no volume control but painted one anyway, so the first time any device reported its volume the repaint threw -- and since the repaint ran inside the poll, that killed the poll thread outright. The card then sat on whatever was playing when it died: it did not notice a skip, did not follow a pause made anywhere else, and only ever showed the song you had started from its own menu. The slider it wanted now exists, painting can no longer take the poll down with it, and a poll that does stop is restartable rather than merely believed to be alive.
Volume is a real control -- a slider on the time row and a speaker that fades toward mute -- where before there was none at all.

"No active device" is no longer the end of the answer. Spotify says that about a desktop app that has merely gone idle or a phone with the screen off, and naming the device in the request wakes it. Play, pause, skip, seek, volume, shuffle, repeat and queue all do that now, so the card works when Spotify is not already open and on screen -- which is what made it look like it only worked from inside its own panel.

An executor that rewrites PUT as POST is detected and said out loud. MacSploit does this, and Spotify answers 405 to every play, pause, volume and like as a result -- which the card reported as 'That did not work', as if it were your fault or Spotify's. It is neither, so it now says which it is, and routes those calls through the MCP bridge when one is running, since a real PUT leaves that process intact.

Connecting can be nothing but a pasted access token. The Client ID and the authorise round trip are still there and still the way to a connection that never expires, but they are no longer the price of trying it once.
Volume sits with the transport now, right of repeat, rather than adrift in the row below it -- it is a playback control, so it belongs with the playback controls.

Every slider has a handle. A three-pixel bar reads as something being reported to you rather than something you can take hold of, and that is true of the scrubber, the volume and all six aim settings at once.

The aim key is yours to choose. Right mouse is a fine default and a poor requirement -- it is the camera in plenty of games, and a phone has no such button -- so the panel now takes whichever input you press, and keeps it.

When an executor sends a request Spotify will not accept, the card says so in words instead of reporting that it did not work, and names what still does. It no longer asks a bridge that is not running, which was costing a pause on every press for everybody who has never run one.

A keybind no longer fires while you are typing. The usual way to ask whether a key was consumed means the GAME consumed it, and every text box here lives in the executor's own UI container, which the game does not own -- so a letter typed into the command bar also reached the hotkeys and toggled things mid-word. It asks who has focus now instead, which is the question it always meant. This is why typing, commands and clicking all felt off on Windows, where that container sits further from the game than it does elsewhere.

Minimised panels are a small square with the panel's mark rather than a full-width bar. Collapsed at 720 pixels wide, the AI panel read as a window that had failed to close instead of one parked out of the way. Drag it, or click it to bring the panel back.

!fontsize sets how big the hub's text is, from a picker or straight from the command. The whole ladder scales together, so headings stay ahead of body text rather than everything meeting in the middle.

Unloading puts your walkspeed and jump back. Everything else in the teardown restored what it changed; these two walked away leaving you fast, with no hub left to slow you down. Click-teleport builds a fresh pair of handlers each time its key goes down, and only dropped them on the matching release -- unloading mid-hold left one alive, so clicking still teleported you.

The Spotify card matches what your executor can actually do. Play, pause, seek, volume, shuffle, repeat and like are one kind of request; skip, previous, queue, search and the playlists are another, and the second kind works everywhere. On an executor that sends the first kind wrong they are shown as unavailable -- dimmed, and they no longer light up under the cursor -- rather than left looking live and failing when pressed, which reads as Spotify being broken when it is one verb on one executor. Connect a bridge and they come back on the next poll.

Spotify search covers artists and albums, not only tracks. One request asks for all three and they come back under their own headings. An artist opens their discography, newest first, so what somebody put out recently is the first thing you see; an album opens its track list; either can be played whole from a button at the top. Their top tracks are not offered because Spotify stopped answering for them in February.

The Spotify panel could get stuck where it would not drag. Every drag starts a per-frame loop that writes the panel's position, and it was never stopped -- so one left over from a rebuild sat there pinning the panel to where it used to be while you tried to move it. The same leak was in every floating panel and the workspace editor; the activity card and the script hub had always done it right.

The startup chime belongs to startup. !overview opens the same screen, so reopening it played the arrival sound again -- a sound that says the hub has just landed, said at a moment when it plainly has not.
The overview shows what is playing, when something is. Cover, track, artist and the device it is on, with a button that pauses it -- or opens the card instead, on an executor that cannot pause.

Friends in the overview are ones you can actually go to. Someone sitting on the website or in the app filled the same two slots every time while friends who were in a game went unshown; they are now kept only when nobody is in a game at all, which is the case where knowing somebody is around is still worth a row.

The now-playing row shows the album cover. It only used one already cached, which at startup is never -- so it drew the disc glyph every time. The slot is shaped up front and the cover fills it whenever the download lands, which moves nothing.
Three friends in the overview rather than two. The column had room for another and was ending short.

!antifling actually works. It cleared collisions once per character and then only for parts that arrived afterwards -- clever, and the reason it did nothing: the Humanoid turns CanCollide back on continuously, and nothing was watching for that. Measured in a live server, two limbs were collidable again within a second and a half of being cleared. It now re-applies every frame the way Infinite Yield does, but from a cached list and only when a part is not already clear: 471 frames of it cost 12 property writes where IY's approach would have cost 8,007.

The now-playing row shows its cover, and appears at launch rather than only when the screen is reopened. Two separate faults: the overview draws once and was drawing before Spotify's first read landed, so there was nothing to show; and the cover was dropped on the way to being drawn, because each row is rebuilt field by field and that field was not on the list.

The Spotify card no longer throws itself in front of the overview at launch. That screen already says what is playing and has a button to open the card, so the card appearing unasked was the hub arguing with itself.
That button opens the card rather than pausing. Pause is the one thing you can already do from wherever else you have Spotify open; the card is the thing you cannot reach any other way.

Every press-T hint names the key that is actually bound. Move it to G and the splash tip, the loaded toast, the bar, the guide and the tour all say G -- and rebinding repaints the bar underneath the control you just used.

The MCP can see the screen. Roblox will not give a script a picture of itself -- the capture API hands back an id whose bytes nothing on the client can read, and several executors refuse the call outright as malicious -- so the bridge takes the picture instead, being a native process looking at the same screen. It arrives as a real image, about a second, and the game says on screen that it happened, because a picture of somebody's screen is taken with them rather than of them.

Two tools for time. wait_for holds on until something becomes true in the game and then answers, instead of guessing how long to sleep. schedule leaves a tool running in the background and keeps what it says -- only what changed -- so a model can watch who joins, or what is playing, while carrying on with the conversation, and read the history later with jobs.

Only reads can be left running. Anything that changes the game owes the user an approval prompt, and a background job is the one thing that cannot stop and wait for one -- so a watch watches, and does not act. wait_for is treated as code rather than as a read, because the condition it compiles is an expression and an expression can call anything.

!mcpinfo says what the far end is connected to, what it may reach for, whether it asks first, how many calls it has made and what it did lately -- the question people actually have about this feature, which is 'is it on, and what can it do to me'.

!mcpsettings decides what an outside model may touch, in five groups rather than twenty tick boxes: reading the game, running commands and code, speaking in chat, Spotify and translation, and waiting or watching in the background. A group that is off is taken out of the list AND refused if something calls it anyway -- a list is a menu, not a lock.

Full auto, behind the same dialog the config wipe uses: a countdown, a dead button, and six lines saying exactly what it means. It lets an outside model run anything without a prompt, and it is deliberately never saved -- it lasts the session, so nobody comes back to a hub already in it.
And a switch for whether tool calls put a toast on screen, for when you are watching it work and do not need telling each time.

The MCP settings look like the rest of the hub. The rows were hand-rolled without a glyph and read as a different product sitting inside the same one; they are the ESP panel's row now -- accent icon, label, description under it, switch on the right -- and each scope carries its own mark.

Four new icons, and a tool that adds them. The interface ships around a hundred Lucide icons rendered white at 64x64, and matching that by hand is easy to get subtly wrong -- a different stroke weight reads as a different icon set. tools/add_icon.py fetches and renders one properly, and can re-render an existing icon to prove it still matches.

The MCP bridge stopped killing itself. It writes a line to its client whenever the toolbox changes, and that write also happens on the thread the game polls -- so with no client attached, the pipe was closed and the first successful poll died with it. It cannot raise there any more.

And it stopped downgrading itself. It kept the published copy for next launch whenever that copy DIFFERED, and GitHub serves the previous file for a minute or so after a push -- so a bridge could quietly be rolled back to the version it had just replaced. It only moves forward now.

entries.title: Quiet movement, anti-fling, chat log
notes: The Da Hood ban warning fired in Brookhaven. Its list of Da Hood place ids had 4924922222 in it, which is Brookhaven -- the hub's own quick-join table says so, in the same file. That id is gone, along with a second one that was typed from memory rather than looked up; a place that is not on the list is now asked about by name instead of assumed. The answer is also remembered against the place it was about, so teleporting out of Da Hood no longer carries its warnings into the next game.

!antifling stops you being flung. Infinite Yield's version clears CanCollide on every other character's descendants every single frame, which is the right idea at the wrong cost and only covers flings that work by touching you. This clears them once per character and again on whatever arrives later, then closes the two holes that leaves: a mover parented into your character is removed, and a velocity written straight onto your root is undone. Off while you are seated or flinging on purpose, so it never fights the game or itself.

A quiet fling type: !fling <player> undetected. It teleports in like !goto does, since the position jump was never the signature, and it uses a mover -- which is not optional. Writing a velocity onto your root does nothing at all, because the physics step undoes a raw write, which is the same reason the flier here uses one. What quiet means is the rest: the mover exists for a third of a second rather than two, it is not named after us so a sweep for our own tag finds nothing, it carries 9e4 rather than 9e7, workspace.FallenPartsDestroyHeight is never touched -- that one is global and readable by every script in the place -- and it stops dead instead of drifting off spinning.

!walkspeed and !jump take the same word in the third slot: quiet leaves the Humanoid property at whatever the game set and moves you the difference each frame, so the property reads normal. The ceiling on it is generous -- 200, or eight times the game's own speed if that is higher -- and the toast says when it clamped. It is an honesty limit rather than a safety one: past a point the property reading 16 stops meaning anything.

!fly takes it too -- !fly undetected. The loudest part of flying was never the speed: a BodyVelocity and a BodyGyro are Instances parented to your root, findable by class without anyone looking at how you move, and PlatformStand is a replicated property read straight off you. The quiet style creates neither and writes neither, driving the CFrame instead, capped at a speed a long fall already reaches. What stays visible is the movement, which no client-side flier can hide.
!goto takes a place word too: behind, front, above, side, or walk, which crosses the gap at running speed rather than arriving all at once.

!chatlog keeps everything said since you executed -- a headshot, who, the exact time, and who was standing close enough to have been part of it. Copy, save and clear. It prunes to the last 800 lines as they arrive, so it stays around 200KB rather than growing into something you notice.

!showchat turns the chat back on in a game that hid it, on either of the two chat systems Roblox ships. !enableshiftlock does the same for shift lock, which games turn off with a property on your own player object.

The command bar suggests who you probably mean rather than listing the roster in join order. Whoever just killed you comes first, then anyone you have just named in a command, then recent chat, then who just joined, with standing nearby as a nudge on top. Kills are attributed by the creator tag, the way Roblox does it -- never guessed from who was closest, which would put the wrong name at the top exactly when you are in a hurry.

Clicking a name in the command bar fills it in and moves on to the next argument. It used to run the command on the spot, so picking somebody off the list was the same gesture as flinging them, with nothing in between to change your mind -- and once that was fixed it stayed on the name, because the completion did not end on a space and the list read it as still being typed. Picking a style word advances the same way, since fling takes seconds after it.

Games that ban for this say so before you run it. In Da Hood the rows for fling, backpack, headsit, drag, noclip, infjump, hipheight, and the Infinite Yield jump power grey out with "Da Hood bans accounts for this" on them. fly, walkspeed and jump keep their command rows and grey out only the styles that are not the quiet one -- writing Humanoid.WalkSpeed is what gets read, and the quiet mode does not write it. Everything else, goto included, is left alone. It is a list rather than a detector, and it is stopped rather than forbidden: the toast offers to run it anyway.

Put the type scale back to 13.5 and 11.5. Rounding them to 13 and 12 was done on the theory that Roblox rasterises glyph atlases at integer sizes -- true of the engine, and not what was happening: those values had been in place for weeks and the text looked right. !fixfont now says which font is actually on screen before it says anything about files, because switching to the built-in one is remembered in the config and survives a rejoin, which looks exactly like the fonts breaking with nothing to check. That swap is no longer the primary button on the toast.

entries.title: sUNC, crisper text, a font repair command, and two more panels you can move
notes: !sunc scores this executor against sUNC's own 86 checks -- the same 86, name for name, so the number is comparable with what sunc.su gives you. All 86 are probed; a fully correct executor scores 100%.

The four that cannot simply be fired are checked on everything checkable without firing them: debug.setstack is given only out-of-range arguments and graded on what it refuses, since a valid one crashes the client; replicatesignal on what it refuses, since firing reaches the server; and getcallingscript and getscriptfromthread on being a real executor closure, because nil is the correct answer from our thread and is also what a stub returns. WebSocket.connect opens a real socket to the public echo host, with a bounded wait and a close on every path out.

Every check must be able to fail for a reason rather than only by throwing, and every check is run against a function that exists, is callable and does nothing -- exactly the fake sUNC was built to catch -- and must refuse it. Both rules fail the build. Four of my own checks were caught by them.

Fixed four Debug checks that failed on every working executor: the three upvalue ones captured an immutable string, which the Luau compiler folds into a constant so the closure ends up with no upvalues at all, and debug.getstack asked for one level up -- which, from inside a pcall, is the pcall itself, a C function it rightly refuses.

No single check can hold the sweep up any more. Probes yield -- request does a real HTTP round trip and WebSocket.connect waits on a handshake, which to a host that never answers does not come back at all, and that stranded the run on its last row. Each one now runs on its own thread against a six-second deadline, and one that does not return is a failure rather than a hang.

Run full becomes Cancel while a sweep is going, and stopping one settles the ring on what actually ran rather than freezing mid-sweep. A stopped run is never saved as this executor's score -- it is a fraction of the checks, and showing it as the last result next time would be worse than showing nothing.

Checks whose real test would do something to the game or the network -- fireclickdetector, request, WebSocket.connect -- score half and the row says exactly why they were not run. Counting an unverifiable pass as a pass is the arithmetic sUNC exists to replace.

The panel is draggable, collapsible and closable. Each check expands as it runs to show what it found and collapses as the next one starts, the log follows along, and the ring spins while there is no honest number to show before counting up to the score. Category tabs appear when it finishes: picking one re-animates the ring to that category alone, and it opens on All with the full score so you can inspect afterwards.

Run custom picks what to test -- searchable, whole categories tick at once, and you can add function names of your own. Copy and Save write the full report. Re-opening !sunc shows the last run for this executor; a saved run from a different executor is ignored rather than shown with a caveat.

The sweep is paced to a fixed twelve seconds however many checks are in it, rather than a fixed step per check -- a custom run of five is no longer over before you have read one, and every row finishes opening before the next asks it to close.

!rexec now says what actually came back when it cannot fetch a build -- a 404 page, a rate-limit notice, a truncated response and a dead connection all used to report the same sentence. It also retries without the cache-busting query string, which is what makes every fetch miss the CDN.

Fixed sUNC reporting every check as "not defined": the lookup used rawget on the script environment, and several executors hand the script a proxy whose __index forwards to the real globals -- rawget walks straight past it. It now indexes normally and searches the script environment, getgenv() and _G in turn, since executors do not all inject into the same table.

Text is no longer pixellated at small sizes. Roblox rasterises a glyph atlas at whole pixel sizes -- ask for 13.5 and it rasterises at one size and scales to another. Two steps of the type scale were fractional (13.5 and 11.5), which is every row title and every grey sub line in the interface. Both are whole numbers now.

The workspace font viewer showed one weight because that is all it ever built: a .ttf holds one face, and the viewer staged the single file you clicked and declared it Regular 400 whatever it actually was.

It now reads the weight out of the filename and gathers every font file beside it that belongs to the same family, so opening any one of Manrope's six weights previews all six -- each line rendered in its own weight, lightest first, with the one you clicked in white. The size samples use the weight you opened rather than the family default.
The preview scrolls, since a family is any number of weights and the pane is 80px tall on a phone.

!fixfont checks the font files on disk, repairs what a re-download can fix, and says which of the three causes rough text actually is -- damaged files, an executor that will not load them, or an executor whose renderer is simply worse at a font it has to rasterise itself. Damaged files were invisible before: the only check was that the file existed, so a truncated download stayed broken for good.
!fixfont builtin swaps to Roblox's own font, which is baked into the client and always draws sharp. !fixfont manrope goes back. The choice is remembered.

The ESP window is now a floating panel like the aim one -- draggable, collapsible to a strip that says how many features are drawing, closable, and it stays where you leave it. Refresh and Clear moved inline.

The aim panel's mode description and bind hint were drawn on top of each other. Fixed, its rows now sit on the same cards the rest of the hub uses, and ESP is one click away from it since the two are used together.

Tabs are one control now instead of five. The info panel, the command list, the script hub, Spotify and sUNC had each grown their own strip at three different heights, in two different greys, and all four width formulas guessed the text as roughly seven pixels a character while every button in the interface measured its own properly -- so a row of tabs never quite lined up with the row of buttons under it. One chip, measured the same way, with the selected look spelled out in one place.

The Spotify card sometimes showed nothing playing until you pressed play inside it. /me/player answers 204 whenever Spotify has no ACTIVE DEVICE, which it very often has not even mid-track -- the desktop app goes idle, a phone locks the screen -- and pressing play is what made a device active. It falls back to currently-playing now, keeping the device, volume, shuffle and repeat it already knew, since that endpoint does not carry them.

The Spotify card can be dragged from anywhere that is not a control, including while it is collapsed. Collapsed it could not be dragged at all: the compact card is one big button covering the whole panel and it swallowed every press. A press only counts as a click if it stayed put.

The aim and ESP panels fit a phone. Both were fixed at 470 and 520 wide, which is wider than a phone is. Both measure against the viewport now, and on a narrow aim panel the sliders drop onto their own line under the description rather than sharing the row with it.

entries.title: One workspace, several accounts
notes: Sign in on a second Roblox account and the hub asks once, before anything else: keep using the config that is already here, or set this account up as new. It shows both accounts side by side -- the one that saved it, with when it was last used, and yours, marked NEW.

Set up as new gives that account its own config file. Theme, prefix, keybind, saved scripts and Spotify sign-in all start clean, and the other account's config is left exactly as it was -- this starts one, it does not take one over.
Tick remember and every account after that is handled the same way without asking. The notification that applies it has a Change button, so it is not a decision you make once and cannot find again.

Asked once and only once. Agreeing is recorded per account rather than by moving ownership, otherwise two accounts on one machine would prompt each other on every other boot. After the answer, the guide or the resume prompt gets its turn as normal -- which of the two depends on what you picked.

entries.title: The aim panel is a panel
notes: The aim window is now draggable, collapsible and closable, and it stays where you leave it between sessions -- the same floating panel the Spotify card and the workspace editor use.
Clicking a mode, a toggle or a colour used to close the window. It was a modal, and changing anything in it rebuilt it from scratch; now only the contents redraw and the window stays put.
!aimbot, !silentaim and !aimassist switch an already-open panel instead of closing it, and re-arm silent aim's hook when you switch into it.

entries.title: Aim
notes: !aim opens a panel with three modes behind one target picker: Assist nudges your aim, Lock holds the camera while you hold the bind, and Silent never moves the camera at all. !aimassist, !aimbot and !silentaim open straight into one of them; !unaim turns it off.

Field of view as a real circle on screen, which turns accent when it has somebody. Smoothness, prediction, team check, wall check, and colour pickers for the circle and the target line -- through the same picker the ESP colours use.
Smoothing is framerate independent. A fixed per-frame lerp snaps twice as hard at 120fps as at 60, which is the difference between an assist and an obvious lock depending on whose machine it runs on.

It targets whoever is nearest your CROSSHAIR rather than nearest to you -- the one you were already closest to pointing at is the one you meant -- and sticky keeps that target while you hold, so somebody crossing in front cannot steal your aim mid-shot.
Prediction leads their velocity and is off by default: leading a hitscan shot is a miss.
Wall check is off by default because it costs a raycast per player per frame, and the panel says so rather than leaving you to find out.

Silent aim is honest about its limits. It answers the game's own hit test rather than moving anything, which only works where the game asks in a way a metamethod hook can reach -- the mode description says so, and an executor that cannot hook says so on the spot instead of failing quietly. Both hooks check the caller so they never lie to the hub's own code, and only answer while you are actually holding the bind with a target.
Settings, bind and colours persist, and are type-checked on the way back off disk -- the config is a file anything can edit.
The slider moved onto UI, so the Spotify scrubber, the volume and every numeric setting here are one implementation of "drag a value between two ends" rather than three.

entries.title: A workspace editor
notes: !workspace (or !files, !editor, !explorer, !fs) opens a file manager for the executor's WHOLE workspace, not just unihub's corner of it. Draggable, collapsible, closable, and it remembers where you put it.

Browse with clickable breadcrumbs, filter the current folder as you type, and open a file to read it. Text files open in an editable box with Save; images render; anything else says why it cannot be shown rather than showing an empty pane.
Create a file with its contents and extension, make folders, rename, duplicate, and run a .lua straight from the tree.
It opens on unihub, because that is what anyone opening it from inside the hub is looking for. The workspace root is one click up, and it remembers where you were after that.

Deleting goes through the same staged confirm the config wipe uses -- it names the full path, says how many items are inside a folder, and waits before the button arms. This reaches every other script's data and nothing here goes to a bin.

Rename is copy-then-delete in that order, so a failed write leaves the original rather than nothing. New names cannot contain a slash: a file goes in the folder you are looking at, not wherever the name says.

Every action is gated on the specific function it needs -- an executor with readfile but no delfile is common -- and one that cannot work is dimmed rather than hidden, so the row does not jump and you can see why.
There are no timestamps, because no executor exposes a stat. Size, kind and extension are everything the filesystem will actually tell us, and a Modified column would have been a fabrication.

Built from the parts that already existed: the shared gradient buttons, the modal, the drag easer, the chrome buttons, and the momentum scroller -- which moved off the Spotify panel onto UI so both use one copy.

Copy became copy-then-paste: pick a file up, open any folder, put it down. It used to duplicate in place, which is the one thing you can already do by pasting without moving. Plus a Path button that copies the full path.

The action row wraps instead of running off the edge. gradButton ships at width 10 and expects the caller to size it, so the wrap check was comparing every button against 10 and Delete sat outside the panel.
Code reads as code: no wrapping, a line-number gutter, and sideways scrolling. A minified JSON wrapped to the pane was one grey paragraph with no structure in it.

The editor shows a cursor. A TextBox with transparent text hides its caret and its selection too, so the highlighted overlay made it impossible to see where you were typing -- it now shows colour while you read and plain text the moment you click in.
Selecting a file no longer rebuilds the whole tree. Two rows retint; the list stays put and keeps its scroll and hover.
Reading a file shows a progress bar. readfile blocks, so the work yields a frame first -- otherwise the bar is shown and hidden without ever being drawn.
A file with an extension nothing recognises is opened raw and judged on its bytes. Refusing on the name hid every .conf, .bak and extensionless file that was perfectly readable.
First-seen and last-edited times per file. Not created/modified: no executor exposes a stat, so those would be invented -- these are what the hub itself observed, and they are labelled that way.
Fonts get a type glyph rather than a shirt, and the panel rebuilds on a theme change like every other card -- owning its own ScreenGui meant nothing else was repainting it.
!refreshconfig re-reads the config from disk and rebuilds, so a change made in the workspace editor two commands over does not need the whole hub re-executed.

Cut, with a scissors glyph. Same clipboard as Copy with a flag; pasting moves, writing the destination before removing the source, and the row dims while it is in flight rather than vanishing on a move you can still cancel.
The breadcrumb trail is also a text field -- click the end of it and type a path. A path that is not a folder is refused rather than silently landing you somewhere else.

Folders can be selected, and therefore deleted. delfolder was wired up from the start, but clicking a folder navigated into it, so a folder could never be the selection and Delete was unreachable for every one of them. Click selects, click again enters, the chevron goes straight in.
JSON auto-formats on open, and the button became the way back: Unformat minifies, Format lays it out again.

Deleting anything belonging to Universal Hub says so in the confirm -- which half comes back on the next execute and which does not -- and the tree marks those files with a dot so you know before you get that far.

An extension nothing recognises still gets an icon. Adding the 'unknown' kind without a glyph left every .bak, .qqq and extensionless file drawing nothing, which reads as a row that failed rather than a file of an unknown type.

Horizontal scrolling works. The momentum scroller replaced Roblox's native one and only ever drove the vertical axis, so the code view's sideways scrollbar did nothing -- shift-wheel and drag now move both.
The wheel sink moved onto UI and both panels claim it, so scrolling the workspace no longer zooms the game out either. Two panels can hold it at once without fighting over the binding.

entries.title: Spotify, connected once
notes: !configurespotify connects Spotify for good. Authorization Code with PKCE, so it renews itself in the background and you never paste anything again -- rather than a token that died after an hour.

PKCE means NO client secret. What sits in the config is a refresh token and a client ID; the hub trades them for a fresh access token a minute before each one lapses, and a 401 mid-session renews and retries instead of telling you to reconnect.
Spotify Premium is required, and the setup modal says so first -- for playback control, as always, and since February 2026 to hold a developer app at all.

Every link in setup has a copy button: the dashboard, the exact redirect URI, and the authorise link built from your Client ID. Paste the whole address bar back; the hub finds the code in it, and says 'access denied' rather than 'no code' when you press Cancel.
The setup fields use the same wash, corner and type as everything else in the modal. They were an opaque slab with a stroke that snapped on when focused, which read as a form bolted onto the design.
SHA-256 and base64url in Lua, because Spotify refuses PKCE's plain method. Verified against FIPS 180-4 vectors and RFC 7636's canonical challenge.

Spotify is a floating panel, not a card: !spotify opens it, you drag it where you like and it stays there, and it collapses to a strip -- cover, track, artist, 0:42 / 3:14. As a card it could only appear after the menu had opened and the column had reflowed, which is the lag it had in both directions.
Covers are real images -- fetched, written and served through getcustomasset, capped at 24 with the oldest evicted, cleared on disconnect.
Without opening the card: !play (resume, or search-and-play by name), !pause, !skip, !back, !vol, !np, !unspotify.

Migrated to Spotify's February 2026 API. PUT/DELETE /me/tracks, GET /me/tracks/contains and both /playlists/{id}/tracks endpoints were removed outright -- liking, the heart state, opening a playlist and adding to one all now use /me/library and /playlists/{id}/items. Search's maximum dropped from 50 to 10.

Now playing is rebuilt: the cover is lifted off the glass with a shadow, the artist is in accent rather than a second grey, and the scrubber runs along the bottom edge advancing every frame instead of twice a second. Transport is solid -- at 17px a stroked triangle is mostly hole -- and every glyph on the row, transport and toggles alike, is normalised to one ink height so a single size really does look level.
Whichever track is playing is marked in Queue, Search and Lists -- accent title, a rule down the edge, and a glyph that tells playing from paused.
A track change raises a toast with the cover in it, the way a player command shows the target's face.

Fixes from real use: the search magnifier sat after your text because UIPadding moves children as well as text; covers were JPEGs written into .png files, which some executors accept and some silently refuse, so some art rendered and some was a blank tile; one cover shared by several rows only ever reached the first of them; the queue showed the same track eight times; and add-to-playlist could send an empty uri list and come back as 'missing required field uris'.
Transport is solid, not hollow: at 17px a stroked triangle is mostly hole. All five glyphs are normalised to one ink height and centred, so a single size on one line really does look level.

Momentum scrolling on every list. Roblox scrolls in discrete jumps on a wheel and gives desktop no inertia at all; the wheel adds velocity and it decays per second rather than per frame, so a throw travels the same distance at 30fps as at 60. Collapsing and expanding animates rather than teleporting between two heights.
Lists no longer jump to the top mid-scroll: a track change repaints every row to move the live mark, and that was resetting the scroll position.
One toast per track, not two. Starting something from the menu announced it, then the poll saw a new track and announced it again -- the poll's version wins because it carries the cover.
The now-playing cover restores its glyph if Roblox refuses the image. Only the small tiles had that fallback, so the big one could sit as an empty rectangle.
The toast's small round slot squares off with rounded corners for album art, and stays a circle for a headshot -- a cover composed to fill a square was losing its corners to it.

Covers that were merely slow to decode were being written off. A single IsLoaded check at two seconds is now a signal plus an eight-second timeout, which is why the 72px card art kept failing while the 38px strip, asking a moment earlier, succeeded.

The like, list, shuffle and repeat glyphs are on the same optical grid as the transport, and the unliked heart is thick enough to survive being drawn at 17px -- it was under a pixel wide and read as missing rather than hollow.
Scrolling a list no longer zooms the game out from under you. The wheel reached Roblox's camera as well as the panel; it is sunk while the pointer is over it and released the moment it leaves.
Repeat-one carries a 1. Rotating a circular arrow 180 degrees to mean repeat-one is a circular arrow.
Like and add-to-playlist moved up beside the title. They sat under the album art, a long way from the transport, reading as part of neither.
The clock/weather card is back in the slot it has always had.

The panel shows itself when something starts playing and steps aside when nothing is; closing it by hand is respected until the track changes. Nothing was polling while it was shut, so it could never do that before.

The panel no longer appears on execute. A ScreenGui is Enabled by default, so building one and parenting an opaque panel into it put the panel on screen the moment the hub loaded -- built now means built, not shown, and auto-show ignores the first poll because something already playing when you execute is not an event.

Scrolling could lock up entirely. The wheel is sunk while the pointer is over the panel, and that was driven by MouseEnter/MouseLeave -- a Leave missed because the gui was disabled under the cursor, or a row destroyed mid-hover while a list reloaded, left the wheel sunk for the rest of the session with scrolling and zoom dead everywhere. It is recomputed from the cursor every frame now, so there is no state to get stuck in.

Shuffle, repeat and play/pause stopped flicking back off. Spotify applies these asynchronously, so the poll a third of a second later still reported the old value and overwrote what you had just pressed -- the value you set now wins for a short window, and yields the moment the server agrees.

The heart reflects your library again. /me/library/contains replaced /me/tracks/contains in February and returns a different shape; every plausible one is read, and 'could not tell' is no longer cached as 'not saved'.

Switching theme no longer freezes an open Spotify panel. Every other card is parented to the hub's own gui and dies with it -- this one owns its ScreenGui, so a rebuild left the old panel on screen with live handlers writing to instances nothing repaints. It is torn down first and put back the way it was.

entries.title: Fling that actually throws people
notes: Fling is rebuilt on the method from Universal Hub MAIN. It goes to them and drives your root through their head on alternating offsets, every frame, carrying a velocity the solver can only resolve by launching somebody. The old one spun you in place and hoped they walked into it.
!fling all works. Fling was never registered as a command that takes a crowd, so the token fell through to a name lookup and answered 'no one matched all' -- while the tips screen advertised it.

You come back. Each throw records where you were standing and returns you there before the next target, so a fling all does not end after one person with you out past the skybox. Stopping mid-throw puts you down too.
A bare !fling still means stand still and fling whoever touches you, which is the only thing the old one was ever good for. Give it a name or 'all' to go and get them.
The kill plane and the seated state are put back on stop, on !stopall, and on unload -- a fling interrupted halfway used to leave the whole game with no kill plane and no UI left to fix it.
Finding nothing is an answer, not a row: a sad face and 'Nothing found' centred in the drawer, at a size you can read, for a misspelt command as well as an empty search.
Scripts already running are greyed in the command bar with a badge, so you can see it before you press rather than after the bar has closed.
Picking a script no longer also runs what you typed as a command.
Three new player tokens, on every command that can take them: nearby (everyone within 100 studs), friends (everyone here off your friends list), and joined (whoever arrived last).

fling all no longer misses people. A throw that failed because they were respawning or had not loaded is retried instead of skipped, nobody is thrown twice, and dying halfway no longer ends the run -- it waits for you to come back and carries on.
Flinging someone already flung this run warns instead of restarting the whole job and abandoning everyone still queued.
A crowd token that names nobody says which one was empty -- 'No one is nearby', not 'no one matched nearby', which reads like a typo.
Fling's notification carries the target's headshot, like every other player command already did.
Fling takes a fourth word: seconds on each target, hinted in the bar like every other valued command. !fling all fly 4.

!sfling is its own command now. Standing still and flinging whoever touches you was a fling TYPE, which it never was -- it has no target, so a player, a crowd token and seconds each all meant nothing for it.
The suggestion list shows every token. It used to keep two while nothing was typed, which hid five of the seven behind already knowing the word.

!introvert (or !hermit, !antisocial, !avoidfriends) leaves the game the moment someone on your friends list joins. !extrovert turns it off, and so does unloading or !stopall -- it is the only thing here that acts on its own, so it cannot be left armed behind you.

Tokens no longer look like players in the suggestion list. Their tile was a circle -- which at that size is what a headshot is -- so a block of them read as a block of people wearing glyphs. Squared off, with a rule under the last one.

entries.title: Mobile, animation packs, and a bar that moves
notes: The bar drags anywhere and remembers where. Cards open downward, or upward when there is no room below.
Dragging has weight everywhere -- the bar, the activity panel and the script hub ease toward the pointer instead of welding to it.
Every card fits the screen it is on. Modals scale to the viewport, drawers to the room actually below them.
Touch: a labelled Commands pill that rides the card stack, tap-away to close the bar, and fly steers from the thumbstick.
Animation packs replicate -- the locomotion is driven through the Animator rather than by editing the Animate script, which only ever changed what you saw.
23 animation packs, resolved to their real animation ids. Twelve executor logos in Info.
vfly, fling, copy, walkto, follow, animpack, clearworkspace, fixanim, rexec.
Fetches carry a cache-buster, so a re-execute gets the newest build instead of the CDN's five-minute-old copy.
The camera's field of view is restored to whatever the game had, not a hardcoded 70.
Search ScriptBlox straight from the command bar: star a result, or open the hub already searched for it. Scripts never displace a command -- typing copy gets you the copy command.
!changelog, and a version that only moves when there is an entry explaining what moved with it.
The hub does not drag -- neither the bar nor the command bar. The floating panels (activity, script hub) still do, as they always have.
Command bar search shows a sweeping bar while it waits on ScriptBlox, and an empty bar offers the scripts you ran most recently -- from the hub or from the bar, same list.
Strings are encrypted now, not just locals renamed -- the published file has no readable text in it at all.
Script hub gains Running and Last used tabs; Last used follows you between games rather than resetting per place.
Command bar: searches the whole line, shows recents and scripts for this game, marks verified and key-locked ones, and says so when there are no results.

Every shipped asset is renamed uhub_*. The executor resolves getcustomasset by FILENAME, not by path, so three scripts each shipping a logo.png fought over the name -- which is why Infinite Yield wore our mark and our splash wore another hub's bird.

entries.title: LITE V2 -- rebuilt, not updated
notes: V2 is not V1 with features bolted on. The interface, the command pipeline and the storage were all rewritten.
One glass design system: every bar, chip, card and modal is built from the same treatment, so the whole thing reads as one product rather than a pile of scripts.
A real command bar -- ranked suggestions, player and mode tokens with aliases, argument hints, and Enter that knows whether to complete or run.
Cards instead of windows: clock, weather, performance, profile and settings all live in one stack that reflows around whatever is open.
Everything persists -- theme, prefix, keybind, favourites, positions, usage -- and survives a teleport.
Ships from GitHub with its own icons and font, downloaded once on first run.
Infinite Yield's command set imported wholesale, so V2 is a superset of what V1 could do.
